questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: The lac operon is an example of:
options: An inducible operon, switched on by the presence of substrate
questions.concept: Lactose induces by inactivating the repressor, whereas the trp operon is repressible, being switched off when tryptophan is abundant. Both illustrate feedback economy in prokaryotes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Real-time quantitative PCR differs from conventional PCR in that it:
options: Measures product accumulation during amplification, allowing quantification
questions.concept: Quantitative PCR is used for HIV and hepatitis viral load monitoring and for measuring minimal residual disease in leukaemia, where absolute quantity guides therapy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis exploits:
options: Sequence variations that create or abolish restriction enzyme sites
questions.concept: RFLP was historically used for sickle cell diagnosis, as the sickle mutation abolishes an MstII site. It has largely been replaced by direct sequencing and allele-specific PCR.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Recombinant human insulin is produced by:
options: Inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria or yeast using a plasmid vector
questions.concept: Recombinant production eliminated the immunogenicity and supply limits of bovine and porcine insulin and enabled engineered analogues such as lispro and glargine with tailored kinetics.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Epigenetic regulation of gene expression includes:
options: DNA methylation and histone modification without change in nucleotide sequence
questions.concept: Promoter hypermethylation silences tumour suppressor genes in cancer, and imprinting disorders such as Prader-Willi and Angelman illustrate epigenetic control. These changes are potentially reversible.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: CRISPR-Cas9 is used in genetic engineering to:
options: Introduce targeted double-strand breaks allowing precise gene editing
questions.concept: A guide RNA directs Cas9 to a specific sequence. Off-target effects and germline editing ethics remain major concerns, though somatic therapy for sickle cell disease and thalassaemia has entered clinical use.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay detects:
options: Antigen or antibody using an enzyme-conjugated detection system
questions.concept: ELISA is highly sensitive and suited to large-scale screening as in HIV and hepatitis testing, which is why it is used as the screening test with a more specific assay for confirmation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: In situ hybridisation differs from blotting in that it:
options: Localises nucleic acid sequences within intact cells or tissue sections
questions.concept: FISH detects HER2 amplification in breast cancer and BCR-ABL1 in leukaemia while preserving tissue architecture, allowing correlation of genetic change with morphology.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Gene therapy for adenosine deaminase deficiency was historically significant because it:
options: Was the first approved human gene therapy trial
questions.concept: Somatic gene therapy alters only the treated individual, whereas germline modification would be heritable and is prohibited in most jurisdictions - a fundamental ethical distinction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Gene regulation & molecular techniques (PCR, blotting)
questions.stem: Northern blotting is used to study:
options: RNA, and therefore gene expression levels
questions.concept: Because it measures transcript abundance it reveals which genes are being expressed in a tissue, complementing Southern blotting which shows only whether the gene is present.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Relative risk is calculated in which study design?
options: Cohort study, as incidence can be measured directly
questions.concept: Case-control studies yield the odds ratio, which approximates relative risk when the disease is rare. Only cohort and experimental designs measure incidence and therefore true risk.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Attributable risk represents:
options: The incidence in the exposed minus incidence in the unexposed, indicating public health impact
questions.concept: Relative risk indicates strength of association and aetiological significance, while attributable risk indicates how much disease could be prevented by removing the exposure - the public health measure.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Confounding is best controlled at the analysis stage by:
questions.concept: At the design stage randomisation, restriction and matching are used. Increasing sample size reduces random error but does nothing about confounding, which is a systematic error.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Recall bias is a particular problem in:
options: Case-control studies, as cases remember exposures differently from controls
questions.concept: Cases search their memory harder for explanations of their illness. Cohort studies avoid it by recording exposure before disease occurs, but are vulnerable to loss to follow-up.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: The Bradford Hill criterion carrying the greatest weight for causation is:
options: Temporality - the exposure must precede the outcome
questions.concept: Temporality is the only absolutely necessary criterion; all others strengthen the argument but none alone proves causation. Strength, consistency, dose-response and reversibility are the next most persuasive.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Number needed to treat is calculated as:
options: The reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction
questions.concept: A smaller NNT indicates greater benefit. It is more clinically meaningful than relative risk reduction, which can appear impressive even when the absolute benefit is trivial.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Lead time bias in screening refers to:
options: Apparent increased survival merely because diagnosis was made earlier, without delaying death
questions.concept: Length bias is the preferential detection of slow-growing indolent disease. Both inflate apparent screening benefit, which is why mortality rather than survival is the valid endpoint in screening trials.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: The healthy worker effect is an example of:
options: Selection bias, where employed populations are healthier than the general population
questions.concept: It biases occupational cohort studies towards the null, potentially masking a genuine hazard. Comparison with other working populations rather than the general population reduces it.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: A p value of 0.03 means:
options: There is a 3 percent probability of observing this result or more extreme if the null hypothesis were true
questions.concept: A p value says nothing about effect size or clinical importance, which is why confidence intervals are preferred as they convey both precision and magnitude of effect.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: A type II (beta) error occurs when:
options: A true difference exists but the study fails to detect it, usually from inadequate sample size
questions.concept: Power equals 1 minus beta, conventionally set at 80 or 90%. Type I (alpha) error is falsely rejecting a true null hypothesis, conventionally limited to 5%.
